falsification.answer: Mechanism is ambiguous and the loss path is unsupported: the packet shows a full-balance outflow with no caller, authorisation context or protocol attribution, and lists zero integrator exposure. An authorised treasury movement or bridge settlement is indistinguishable on this evidence.

ai.narrative: A contract on Ethereum had its entire USDC balance, 4,000,000 USDC (about $3,998,911), moved out in one transaction. That is 100% of what it held. Beyond that, the packet tells us nothing: no protocol name, no attacker or authorised-signer context, no function called, and no integrators listed as exposed. A treasury sweep, a bridge settlement or a contract migration produces exactly this shape on chain. Without a caller or authorisation signal there is no basis to call this an exploit, and no identified counterparty whose loss we could trade against.
ai.lossBearer: Not established. The only identified party is the drained contract 0xa2cf...9913; no protocol, depositor base or integrator exposure is shown in the packet.

ai.narrative: A single Ethereum transaction moved 19,652,782.262853 USDT out of contract 0x1601843c5e9bc251a3272907010afa41fa18347e, about 64% of that balance. That is the entire substance of the evidence. There is no trace of who called it, no permission change, no failed access check, and no named protocol or product behind the address. A treasury sweep, a bridge settlement or a scheduled migration would look exactly like this on chain. The packet also reports drained exposure of $57,397,377 against a $19,652,782 single-asset move, and that gap is not explained. Nothing here establishes an unauthorised loss path, so I am not endorsing a trade on it.
